title: the iron Bhima
hookLine: a blind king asks to embrace the man who killed his sons, and Krishna slides an iron statue into his arms
carry: moha: blind love for what's mine
tomorrow: will Gandhari curse the men who won?

lines: THE PANDAVAS COME TO MEET HIM.
cards: A line of chariots and carts leaves Hastinapura, and behind it walk the women of the royal house, weeping, their hair unbound. They're going out to the battlefield to find their dead.
At the front is Dhritarashtra, the blind old king, with Gandhari beside him. On the road, the Pandavas come to meet him: the five brothers who won, with Krishna. They bow.
The king has to greet them. And he asks for one of them in particular.

teach.b: Dhritarashtra embraces Yudhishthira first, the text says, without joy. Then he asks for Bhima, the one who killed Duryodhana and Duhshasana. Krishna understands what's in the old man's heart.
He quietly pushes Bhima aside and moves forward an iron statue of Bhima, which Duryodhana had made, in Ganguli's telling, to practice against with his mace.
The blind king takes the iron figure in his arms and crushes it, so strong with grief and rage that it breaks apart, and he hurts himself. He falls, and Sanjaya lifts him up.
Then he weeps for Bhima, sure he has killed him. Krishna speaks. It was only an image of iron, he says, in effect.

teach.h: "YOUR SONS DIED BY THEIR OWN DEEDS"
teach.b: Your sons died by their own deeds, and because you didn't stop them. The king is ashamed, and maybe relieved. He washes, and embraces the brothers, Bhima too, with blessings this time.

Hindus have a word for what blinded this king long before today: moha, the love that clings to what's mine until it can't see straight. His eyes were blind from birth, but many teachers say this was his deeper blindness.

The Gita opens with his voice asking what my sons and Pandu's sons did, and teachers often point to that one word, my, as the whole war in seed. It ends with Arjuna saying, my moha is gone. Krishna doesn't shame the king.
He gives the grief iron to break, then names the truth. Moha isn't too little love.

teach.h: MOHA: LOVE THAT ONLY SEES MINE
teach.b: It's love that only sees mine.

how: The iron Bhima appears in retellings of the Stri Parva as a picture of a father's moha and of Krishna's foresight, and 'idam na mama', this is not mine, is said with offerings in many Hindu fire rituals.

o: the queen who walks beside the blind king to the field
the book of the women, where grief breaks an iron Bhima
the iron image Duryodhana had made for his practice

games.q: on the road — tap the pairs.

s: Dhritarashtra crushed Bhima in his embrace
Krishna slipped an iron statue into his arms, and the king crushed that.
Duryodhana had the iron statue made to practice against
it was an iron image of Bhima for his mace practice.
moha means having too little love
moha is love that clings to 'mine' until it can't see; the king loved his sons blindly.

games.q: you're Krishna. the blind king, wild with grief, asks to embrace Bhima, and you can see what's in his heart. what do you do?
o: push Bhima aside and move the iron statue forward.
refuse the embrace in front of everyone.
games.why: Krishna moves the iron Bhima forward, the king's grief breaks on iron, and then Krishna names the truth his moha couldn't see.

practice: At a Hindu fire offering, as each spoonful of ghee goes into the flame, the words are often idam na mama: this is not mine. Make two fists slowly, holding something you love tightly in your mind, a person, a plan, a side you're on.
Breathe in and feel the grip. Breathe out and open your hands, palms up, as if setting it into the fire: not mine. If you pray, you can offer that person to God with open hands.
If you don't, just let the hands stay open.

wordCard.voice: Stri. In the book of the women, a blind king's moha breaks an iron Bhima, and only then can he embrace the living one.

orig.note: moha: the clinging love that blinds; at the end of the Gita, Arjuna says his is gone.

carryVoice: Your line: moha, blind love for what's mine. Tomorrow, Gandhari, and the men who won. See you then.
